title: String Methods
description: Built-in tools for measuring, cleaning and reshaping text.

content.text: A pocket knife carries its tools with it. Every string does too. You open a tool with a dot, then its name and `()`. Tools that work this way are called **methods**.

parts.label: the string
parts.note: The text you want to work on.

parts.label: dot
parts.note: Means: use one of this string's tools.

parts.label: call
parts.note: Parentheses run the tool. Some methods take values inside them.

items: One measuring tool is written differently: `len()`.
It **wraps around** the string instead of following a dot.
It counts **every** character, including spaces and punctuation.
content.title: Counting with len()

content.value:
message = "Hello World"

print(len(message))      # five letters, a space, five letters
print(message.upper())

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `len()` counts every character. `"Hi! "` has `H`, `i`, `!` and a space at the end, so the answer is `4`.

items.sub: First Letter Of Each Word Capital

content.caption: `.title()` is handy for tidying a name somebody typed in a hurry.

steps.label: User types `YeS`
steps.detail: People type in all sorts of ways.

steps.label: `True`
steps.detail: No need for a condition per spelling.

content.value: Type some text below and try each tool on it.

items: `.strip()` removes spaces from the very **start** and **end**.
Spaces in the middle are left alone.
Use it on anything a person typed: a stray space at the end is invisible, but still breaks a comparison.
content.title: strip()

items.title: Without strip
items.text: `False`. The extra spaces make the strings different.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `.strip()` removes the spaces at both ends, so only `hi` is left between the brackets.

items: `.replace()` swaps one piece of text for another.
Give it two things: what to look for, and what to put in its place.
**Every** match is swapped, not just the first.
content.title: replace()

parts.label: put instead
parts.note: The text that goes in its place.

content.value:
sentence = "I like apples and apples"
print(sentence.replace("apples", "cookies"))

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `.replace()` swaps **every** `a`, not just the first one.

content.value: A string method **never changes** the string it was called on. It builds a new string and hands it back. Calling a method on its own line achieves nothing. If a method seems to do nothing, check that you stored the result or used it inside `print`.
content.title: This catches people out

content.code:
message = "hello"
message.upper()
print(message)
message = message.upper()
print(message)

steps.note: `.upper()` builds `"HELLO"`, but nothing stores it, so it is thrown away. `message` is unchanged.
This time the new string is assigned back to `message`, so it is kept.
Now the box holds the capital version.

content.title: Kept or thrown away?
content.outro: Store the result, or use it straight away inside `print`.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: Line 2 builds `CAT` but never stores it, so `pet` still holds `cat`.

editorCode:
secret = "  python is awesome  "

print("Length:", len(secret))
print(secret.strip().upper())
print(secret.replace("python", "coding").strip())
print("Original is unchanged:", secret)

quiz.question: Which tool gives the number of characters in a string?
quiz.explain: len() counts the characters, spaces included. It wraps around the string rather than following a dot.

quiz.question: What does  "  hi  ".strip()  give you?
quiz.explain: .strip() removes the spaces at the start and end only. Spaces in the middle of the text are left alone.

quiz.question: What is printed?  message = "hello"  /  message.upper()  /  print(message)
quiz.explain: The capitals were built and then thrown away, because the result was never stored. message itself never changed.
